title: How to Calculate a 6 Figure Salary: Hourly Rate, Fortnightly Pay, Tax and Super
description: Learn how to convert an hourly rate to a 6 figure salary using 38-hour weeks. Includes casual loading, super on top, tax brackets, and fortnightly pay estimates.
salarySummary: For a 38-hour week, a 6 figure salary of $100,000 per year equates to an hourly rate of approximately $50.61 before tax and super.

faqs.q: Does a casual employee on a 6 figure salary also get casual loading and super on top?
faqs.a: Yes. Casual loading (usually 25%) is added to the base hourly rate before calculating annual pay. Superannuation of 12% is paid on top of ordinary earnings, not included in the salary figure. For example, a base rate of $50.61/hour becomes $63.26/hour with casual loading, and the employer pays an additional $6.07/hour in super.

faqs.q: What tax does a 6 figure salary attract in 2026–27?
faqs.a: For a $100,000 annual salary, the 2026–27 resident tax is $18,200 tax-free, then 15% to $45,000, then 30% to $135,000. The tax on $100,000 is approximately $24,967 plus Medicare levy of 2% ($2,000), total around $26,967. This estimate does not include HELP or Medicare levy surcharge or salary packaging.

faqs.q: How do I convert a 6 figure salary to fortnightly pay?
faqs.a: Divide the annual salary by 26 to get weekly pay, then multiply by 2 for fortnightly. For $100,000, weekly is $3,846.15, fortnightly is $3,846.15. For an hourly rate of $50.61/hour, weekly is $1,923.08, fortnightly $2,000.

bodyMarkdown:
## Understanding the 6 Figure Salary

A 6 figure salary is any annual pay of $100,000 or more. For a full-time employee working a standard 38-hour week, the hourly rate needed is about $50.61 per hour. This guide explains the calculation, casual loading, super on top, tax, and superannuation using the latest Fair Work Ombudsman and Australian Taxation Office information.

## The Basic Calculation: Hourly × Hours × 52

The formula is simple: hourly rate × hours per week × 52 weeks. We assume 38 hours per week as the standard full-time week under the National Employment Standards. For a 6 figure salary of $100,000, the hourly rate is $100,000 ÷ (38 × 52) = $50.61. This assumes the same rate every week, no unpaid overtime, no penalty rates, no allowances, and no salary sacrifice.

If you work more or fewer hours, adjust the hours per week. For example, a 40-hour week gives $48.08 per hour for $100,000. The [hourly conversion](/topics/hourly-conversion) tool on this site can help.

## National Minimum Wage and Award Rates

The National Minimum Wage from 1 July 2026 is $26.44 per hour, or $1,004.90 per week for 38 hours. Many employees are covered by an award that sets higher minimum rates. The Fair Work Ombudsman publishes [pay guides](/blog) that list minimum pay rates, allowances, and penalty rates for each award. These guides are the authoritative source for your minimum entitlement. If you are on a 6 figure salary, you are well above the minimum, but your award may still affect overtime and penalty rates.

## Casual Loading and Super on Top

Casual employees receive a 25% loading on top of their base hourly rate to compensate for lack of paid leave. The base rate is the award or minimum rate. For a 6 figure salary, the base rate of $50.61 becomes $63.26 per hour with casual loading. The [casual loading page explains the details. The loading is not included in the salary figure.

Superannuation is paid on top of ordinary earnings. From 1 July 2026, employers must pay super each payday under the Payday Super rules. The super guarantee is 12% of ordinary earnings, up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830. For a $100,000 salary, super is $12,000 per year on top. This is not deducted from your pay; it is an additional cost to the employer. The [super and packaging](/topics/super-and-packaging) page has more detail.

## Tax and Medicare

For the 2026–27 financial year, the resident tax rates are:
- Nil on the first $18,200
- 15% on the next $26,800 (to $45,000)
- 30% on the next $90,000 (to $135,000)
- 37% on the next $55,000 (to $190,000)
- 45% above $190,000

Medicare levy is generally 2% of taxable income. For a $100,000 salary, tax is approximately $24,967 and Medicare $2,000, total $26,967. This estimate uses the 2025–26 Medicare reduction thresholds because the 2026–27 thresholds were not confirmed. HELP, Medicare levy surcharge, and salary packaging are not included.

## Fortnightly Pay

Fortnightly pay is weekly pay multiplied by 2. Weekly pay is annual salary divided by 52. For $100,000, weekly is $1,923.08, fortnightly is $3,846.15. For an hourly rate of $50.61, weekly is $1,923.18, fortnightly $3,846.36. This helps with budgeting.

## Annualised Wages and Salary Offsetting

Some awards and enterprise agreements allow annualised wages where a fixed amount covers minimum pay, penalties, overtime, allowances, and annual leave loading. The Fair Work Ombudsman explains that an annualised wage must not be less than what the employee would have received under the award. Employers must review the arrangement every 12 months and pay any shortfall. Salary offsetting in an employment contract can also cover entitlements, but the employer must still pay in full each period and at least monthly. These arrangements are common for 6 figure salaries to simplify payroll.

## Using the Timesheet

Our [timesheet](/) lets you enter a base hourly rate and optionally add 25% casual loading. It calculates annual, weekly, fortnightly, monthly pay, tax, Medicare, and super. Never enter a rate that already includes casual loading; use the checkbox instead. The results are estimates based on the assumptions above.

## Summary

A 6 figure salary of $100,000 per year requires about $50.61 per hour for a 38-hour week. Casual loading adds 25% on top of the base rate. Super is 12% on top of ordinary earnings. Tax and Medicare reduce take-home pay. Use the [pay guides](/blog) for your award, the [minimum wage](/topics/minimum-wage) page for current rates, and the [take-home pay](/topics/take-home) page for net estimates. Always check with the Fair Work Ombudsman and the Australian Taxation Office for your specific situation.
